summary: Describes the H ratio, a measure of how efficiently an address space is used when assigning addresses. It was submitted to the IPng effort to help judge address-assignment schemes. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: When choosing how many bits an address should have, people asked how full the address space would be. This memo argues that the plain ratio is misleading and proposes a logarithmic measure instead, then uses it to conclude that 128 bits is plenty.

questions: is 128 bits enough for ipv6 addresses
how is address space utilization measured
subtitle: A logarithmic yardstick for how efficiently an address space is actually used.

tldr.problem: During the IPng debate people judged address plans by "assignment efficiency", but the plain ratio of systems to possible addresses is misleading because addresses are arranged in a hierarchy.
tldr.mechanism: The memo proposes H = log(number of objects) divided by available bits, using base 10 logs, so H runs from 0 to a theoretical maximum of 0.30103.
tldr.outcome: Real numbering plans show H usually between 0.14 and 0.26, and on that basis the author concludes that 128 bits is more than enough.

today: RFC 1715 is an Informational memo. The unit metadata lists RFC 3194 as updating it, and no RFC as obsoleting it.

sections.title: Efficiency of Address Assignment
sections.content:
The memo was submitted to the IETF IPng area in response to RFC 1550. Publication does not imply acceptance by the IPng area of any ideas expressed in it.

Most people in the debate expressed assignment efficiency as the ratio of the effective number of systems in the network to the theoretical maximum. On that measure, the 32-bit IP addressing plan, with about 3.5 million addresses reported in the DNS, gives an efficiency of 0.05%. The author calls this classic evaluation misleading, because it does not take into account the number of hierarchical elements; IP addresses, for example, have at least three degrees of hierarchy: network, subnet and host.
sections.plainLanguage: The old way to judge an address plan was to count real devices and divide by the largest number the space allows. That makes working systems look wasteful, because addresses are split into groups and subgroups.

sections.title: The H Ratio
sections.content:
To remove the dependence on hierarchy, the memo proposes a logarithmic scale: H = log (number of objects) / available bits. The ratio H is not very dependent on the number of hierarchical levels: two levels of 8 bits each with about 100 elements per level give the same efficiency as a single level of 16 bits with about 10000 elements.

The memo uses base 10 logs because they are easier to compute mentally and because people describe large numbers in powers of ten. With that choice, H varies between 0 and a theoretical maximum of 0.30103, the log base 10 of 2.
sections.plainLanguage: The proposed score divides the number of digits in the count of objects by the number of bits available. Splitting the space into levels does not change the score much, and the score can never exceed about 0.30103.

sections.title: Values Seen in Practice
sections.content:
The author looks at the moment when several numbering plans broke and had to grow. Adding a digit to French telephone numbers when the number of phones reached 1.0 E+7 gives 0.26. Expanding the US telephone system to about 10 digits for 1.0 E+8 subscribers gives about 0.24. The 32-bit Internet with about 3 million hosts gives 0.20, rising to 0.23 if the number of hosts grows tenfold. SITA's fixed-length addresses give 0.14, the physics/space science DECnet Phase IV stopped at about 15K nodes for a ratio of 0.26, and about 200 million IEEE 802 nodes in a 46-bit space give 0.18.

From these examples the memo asserts that the efficiency ratio usually lies between 0.14 and 0.26.
sections.plainLanguage: The author checks telephone and computer networks at the moment they ran out of room, and finds they were all similarly full, between about one seventh and about one quarter of the theoretical maximum.

sections.title: Evaluating Address Plans
sections.content:
Working in reverse at the pessimistic ratio of 0.14 and the optimistic ratio of 0.26 gives population counts for each address size: 32 bits supports 3 E+4 to 2 E+8, 64 bits supports 9 E+8 to 4 E+16, 80 bits supports 1.6 E+11 to 2.6 E+27, and 128 bits supports 8 E+17 to 2 E+33.

The author says this explains why some feel 64 bits is "not enough" while others call it sufficient, and concludes that 128 bits is "more than enough": even at the lowest efficiency it is far above the hyperbolic estimate of 1.E+15 Internet hosts. The memo says security issues are not discussed.
sections.plainLanguage: Depending on how full an address space is expected to get, a medium size may look too small or generous, while the largest size is safe either way. The memo does not discuss security.
